Annual Meetings

Afternoon Session - 2008 Meeting

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger sound the alarm about financial firms that have taken on too much risk to manage, but are "too big to fail." Buffett also identifies what he thinks is the "primary problem of mankind," and Munger calls the housing bubble a "particularly foolish mess."

Sat, May 3 2008 • 1:00 PM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 2. "Too big to fail" banks can't have "too much risk to manage"
  2. 4. Buffett on religion: "I'm a true agnostic"
  3. 8. "If we can't make a decision in five minutes, we can't make it in five months"
  4. 13. Nuclear proliferation is the "primary problem of mankind"
  5. 18. Munger on housing: A "particularly foolish mess"
  6. 23. Disagreement on danger of CDOs

2. "Too big to fail" banks can't have "too much risk to manage"

WARREN BUFFETT: And we'll go onto number 8.

Sync Video to Paragraph

AUDIENCE MEMBER: My name is Ola Larson (PH). I live in Salt Lake City. And I think â on Lou Rukeyser, Wall Street Week, 1981 or something. So you must really have impressed me, Warren.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What I'd like to ask you is that looking at the future, have the business practices of the investment banks become so complex that it is not possible for the head of the investment bank to be aware of the exposures to financial risks day-to-day or week-to-week?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. That's an exceptionally good question, and I think the answer, probably, is yes, at least in some places, although there's a few investment bank heads I've got enormous respect for their ability to sort of get their minds around risk.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But I decided, for example, when we bought Gen Re, it had about 23,000 derivative contracts, and I think I could have spent full time on that and not really been able to get my mind around how much risk we could â we were running â under some fairly extreme conditions that I did not think were impossible, but that the people who were running the operation might have thought were impossible, or that might not have cared about it that much because their own incentive compensation was such that if they made a lot of money one year on something, it would work 99 years out of a hundred, they would feel the chances of something going wrong big were very slim.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But I don't want to have it slim. I want to have it none. So I regard myself as the Chief Risk Officer at Berkshire.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If something goes wrong at Berkshire because of â in terms of risk â of the way we run the place, there's no way I can assign that to a risk committee or have some mathematicians come in and make a bunch of calculations and tell me I'm only running a risk that will happen once in the history of the universe or something of the sort.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I think the big investment banks, a number of them â and big commercial banks â I think they're almost too big to manage effectively from a risk standpoint in the way they've elected to conduct their business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And it's going to work most of the time. So you don't see the risk in a way that â I mean, you don't â if you have a 1 in 50-year risk that a place will go broke, it may not be in the interest of a 62-year-old executive that's going to retire at 65 to worry too much about that.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I worry about everything at Berkshire. So I would say they're too â they're very hard to manage, very hard to have your mind around. I mean, clearly, you've seen cases in the last year where very big institutions, if the CEO knew what was going on, he certainly hasn't admitted it subsequent to what's happened.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's embarrassing either way, but it's less embarrassing to say I didn't know what was going on than to acknowledge that you knew these kind of activities were going on and you let them go on.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's â I've been asked for advice on regulation sometimes, and we've seen an extraordinary example, which somehow the press really hasn't picked up on much.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But you had an organization called OFHEO whose sole job was to supervise two big companies, and these big companies were Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And they had a large element of public purpose in them, and they were chartered by the federal government, and they had â their activities had overtones for the whole mortgage and securities markets.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So Congress said, "If we're going to give you all this 'too big to fail'-type protection, in terms of the federal government stepping in and giving you special privileges, we want to keep an eye on you."

Sync Video to Paragraph

So they formed OFHEO and they had 200 people going to work, I presume at 9 o'clock every morning, and going home at 5, and their sole job was to see what these two places were doing. And they turned out to be two of the biggest accounting misrepresentations in the history of the world.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So they were two for two with the only things they had to examine. And I fear that if you tried to do the same thing with the biggest commercial banks or the biggest investment banks, I'm not sure you can keep track of it.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What you need is somebody at the top whose DNA is very, very much programmed against risk. And he is going to have to resist the entreaties of those who work beneath him who say everybody else is doing it, and if they can do it over there and make all this money doing it, why can't we be doing it here?

Sync Video to Paragraph

And that's not easy to do. When you've got a bunch of high-powered people who are used to making in seven figures every year, and they want to do things and they say, "If you don't do them here, we're going to go elsewhere," it's a very tough system to be.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So I would say that, in many ways, there are firms that, in terms of risk, are simply â they are conducting themselves in a way that they're too big to manage.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if at the same time the government says they're too big to fail, that has some very interesting policy implications.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, I would argue that you say that very well. It does have interesting policy implications.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's crazy to have people get so big and so important that you can't allow them to fail, and allow them to be run with as much knavery and stupidity as permeated the major investment banks.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

I would argue it's quite counterproductive for the country, and it ought to be reigned way back.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And it's amazing how few people spoke against it as it was happening. There was just so much easy money to be reported.

And only by just total directive could we stop our own employees from trading with Marc Rich.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

3. Why we don't do 'due diligence' for even the biggest deals

WARREN BUFFETT: Well, let's go on to number 9.

Sync Video to Paragraph

AUDIENCE MEMBER: Harry Beguy (PH), San Francisco.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Mr. Buffett, I was reading recently in Fortune magazine that when you invested $500 million in PetroChina back in 2001 or 2002, all you did was read the annual report.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, I was thinking that most professional investors with the kind of resources that you have would have liked to have done a lot more research and talked to management, maybe regulators, et cetera, et cetera.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The question I have is, how â what is it that you look for when you're reading an annual report like that? How is it that you were able to, and did, make an investment purely on the back of reading that report?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. Well, it was in 2002 and 2003, and the report came out in the spring, and I read it. And that's the only thing I ever did. I never contacted any management. I never got a brokerage report. I never asked for anybody's opinion.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But what I did do is I came to the conclusion that the company â and it's not hard to understand crude oil production and refining and marketing and the chemical operation they have. I mean, you can do the same thing with Exxon or BP or any of them, and I do that with all â I look at them.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I came to the conclusion it was worth a hundred billion, and then I checked the price and it was selling for 35 billion, roughly.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What's the sense of talking to management? I mean, basically, if you talk to management of almost every company, they'll say they think their stock is a wonderful buy, and they'll give you all the good stuff and skip over things that â it just doesn't make any difference.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, if I thought the company was worth 40 billion and had been selling for 35 billion, then at that point you have to start trying to refine your analysis more. But there's no reason to refine your analysis.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mean, I didn't need to know whether it was worth 97 billion or 103 billion if I was buying it at 35 billion.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So any further refining of analysis would be a waste of time when what I should be doing is buying the stock.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So we really like things that you don't have to carry out to three decimal places, you know.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If you have to carry it out to three decimal places, it's not a good idea. And, you know, it â with something like PetroChina â it's like if somebody walked in the door here and they weighed somewhere between 300 and 350 pounds. I might not know how much they weigh, but I would know they were fat. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

That's all I'm looking for, is something that's financially fat. And whether PetroChina weighed 95 billion dollars or 105 billion didn't make much difference. It was selling for 35 billion. If it had been selling for 90, it would have made a difference.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So if you can't make a decision on something like PetroChina off the figures, forget about going further, and that's basically what we did. It's a straightforward report, just like reading another â just like reading Chevron's or ConocoPhillips or something like that. Just as informative.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And you weren't going to learn more, you know, by going out and deciding whether you thought â they've got one huge field in China where the life of it was 13 years or 14 years or something of the sort. They should hit you between the eyes.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah. I would argue that we have lower due diligence expenses than anybody else in America â (laughter) â and that we have had less trouble because we had less expense.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I know of an investment operation in America that pays over $200 billion a year that â

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Two-hundred million.

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: 200.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Million.

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yes. 200 million. Pardon me.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Uh-huh.

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: â every year to its accountants, a lot to help them with due diligence.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I think our operation is safer because we think like engineers. We want these margins of reliability. And they're trying to do something really difficult, which is to have fine-grain judgments in very complex areas, and rely on other people to do it who are getting paid fees.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's a very dicey process to do that. I think it's much safer to do our way.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: If you think the auditors know more about making an acquisition than you do, you ought to take up auditing and let them run the business, as far as we are concerned.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We are not â I mean, when we get a call on something like the Mars-Wrigley situation, if we don't know enough about Mars and Wrigley by this point so that we have to go out â I still like to go out, of course, and sample all the bars.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So we have a 15 â I mean, I feel I owe that to the Berkshire shareholders (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

But I'm not going to look at their labor contracts or their leases or anything like that.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If the value of Wrigley depends on a specific lease someplace or a specific commitment to this or that, you know, or a given environmental problem, forget it, you know.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The â there are these overriding considerations that are enormously important, and then there's a whole lot of trivia that doesn't mean anything.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We have never made a â we've made plenty of big investment â I've made plenty of big investment mistakes. I've never made one, in my view, that would have been avoided by conventional due diligence.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And we would have spent a lot of money, and we would have wasted a lot of time and, in some cases, we would have missed deals, simply because we wouldn't have committed fast enough.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We have a significant advantage, and it gets bigger as we get bigger, because, in terms of big deals, people rely more and more often on process, in that when people want to get a deal done, they want to know it's going to be done, they will come to us.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mean, the Mars people wanted to deal â in terms of this financing aspect of the Wrigley situation â they only wanted to deal with Berkshire because they knew we didn't have any lawyers involved. I'll admit to this group we didn't even have any directors involved.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We just â you know, we got a call, it made sense, and we said yes. And when we say yes, we don't say yes with a material adverse change clause. We don't say yes, if financing is available. We just say yes.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So I can tell people when we make a deal that, if we're going to have 6 1/2 billion available, it's going to be available, you know, whether there's a nuclear bomb goes off in New York City, or whether there's a flu epidemic, or whether Ben Bernanke runs off to South America with Paris Hilton. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

The check is going to clear.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if you're making a deal, you know, the guy that wants the 6 1/2 billion, that assurance is worth something. And you really can't get anyplace â they say, "Well, I'll do it, but I've got to have a due diligence team check this out and do all of that." So it's a real advantage to us, and I don't think there's any disadvantage to us.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But when you get into instruments â I've used this illustration before â but when you get into a CDO-Squared, if you read a standard mortgage â residential mortgage-backed certificate â security â it may consist of thousands of mortgages backing up this instrument.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And then that instrument may be traunched into 30 or so different traunches where each party has a different claim on the waterfall of funds received.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, that instrument itself can be kind of difficult to understand. But then you take that and you create a CDO by taking some of the lower junior tranches of a bunch of these RMBSs, maybe 50 of them, and then you create a CDO out of this.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So now you create, out of a whole bunch of junior â and perhaps â and very correlated â and perhaps kind of lousy instruments â and then you put them in a CDO and say that because you put them all together and diversified, in theory, you've got a lot of triple-A traunches of that â was a big error to start with.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And then when you took the lower tranches of a bunch of CDOs and stuck them into a CDO-Squared, that was nuttiness squared.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if a residential mortgage-backed security had a 300 page prospectus and you had to read 50 of those to understand a CDO, you're up to 15,000 pages.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if you had to read 50 more CDO prospectuses, and the material behind that, to evaluate a CDO-Squared, you had to read 750,000 pages, presumably, to evaluate one security, and that was madness.

Sync Video to Paragraph

To let people value that sort of thing, because they say the market at ten cents on the dollar is unrepresentative, so instead of using that, I'll use the hundred cents I paid, I think would be an abomination.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I think that the discipline, mild as it may be, of telling managements that you're going to have to value this stuff at market may keep them from doing things that they would otherwise do that would be very stupid if they think they can get away with valuing them at some fictitious â or at cost â which would be fictitious, in terms of markets.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I lean toward the market value approach. I don't know â when you get into really complex instruments â I just don't know how you value them.

Charlie was on the audit committee at Salomon, and they would spend hours and hours and hours â and I think you found one that was mismarked by 20 million or something like that, back when 20 million was real money.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Well, the answer is I do believe in dividends in a great many situations, including many of the ones at companies in which we own stock.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The test about whether to pay dividends is whether you can continue to create more than one dollar of value for every dollar you retain.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And there are many businesses â take See's Candy, which we own. See's Candy has paid everything, virtually, out to us that they earn because they do not have the ability within See's Candy to use large sums, which they earn, intelligently in their business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So it would be an enormous mistake for See's Candy to retain money. So they distribute to Berkshire, and we hope that we move that around in some other area where that dollar becomes worth $1.10, or $2.10, in terms of present value terms.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If we do that, the shareholder â whether they're taxable or whether they're not taxable, whether they're a foundation or whether they're living on income, even â they are better off if we retain the money.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Because if they were going to get a dollar in dividends and it became worth $1.10 or $1.20 in market value immediately on a present value basis, they're better off selling a small percentage of their stock and realizing the required amount that way, and they will have more money when they get all through doing that than if we paid it in dividends.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But if the time comes â and it will come someday â when the â if the time comes when we don't think we can use the money effectively to create more than a dollar of market value per dollar retained, then it should be paid out.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And, like I say, we do that individually within Berkshire. But because we have this ability to redistribute money in a tax-efficient way within the company, we probably had more â we had more reason â to retain all of our earnings.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If See's Candy were a standalone company, we would simply pay out a lot of the earnings, practically all of the earnings, in dividends. Just like we do now, except it goes to Berkshire.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We like our â we like the companies in which we have investments to pay to us the money they can't use efficiently in their own business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

In some cases that's a hundred percent of what they earn; in some cases it's 0 percent of what they earn. We own some stocks that don't pay any dividends.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Costco paid a very small â did they pay any dividend for a while, Charlie, or â?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: They â while they were growing very rapidly, they paid no dividend. And finally they are paying one.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Berkshire's policy is much the same. Warren has always planned on paying large dividends out of Berkshire, and he does it in the mode of Saint Augustine when he said, "God give me chastity, but not yet."
